newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ad execs find local culture key to global success.
newsitem.headline: Ad execs find local culture key to global success.

text.p: Local tastes and cultures are becoming increasingly important for advertisers and their ad agencies, replacing the notion that products can be marketed around the world with a single ad campaign, advertising executives said.
Advertising executives told Reuters at the six-day International Advertising Festival in Cannes last week that some ideas worked around the world, but most needed to be adapted to local markets.
"There are only local markets. There are no global markets," Michael Conrad, vice chairman of the Chicago-based ad Leo Burnett ad agency, said in an interview.

"The advertising industry has long subscribed to the catch phrase "think global, act local," coined by Theodore Levitt in 1983. That approach has not necessarily been dropped, but the industry has found it is not always an easy or appropriate concept to put into practice.

From agency to agency at the 44th Annual International Advertising Festival, the industry's most important gathering for its creative staffs, the emphasis was on the need to promote brand-name products.

Ogilvy & Mather, owned by WPP Group Plc, the world's largest advertising and marketing services group, calls its approach "brand stewardship". London-based Bartle, Bogle, Hegarty talks about "brand vision". Leo Burnett stresses "brand value".

The power of brand-name products, ranging from Coke and Pepsi to Nike and Kodak, is all about winning the loyalty of consumers around the world in increasingly competitive markets offering a vast number of consumer goods.

"The phrase 'think global, act local' -- I think that's right," Petter Gudmunseth, chairman of JBR/McCann, part of Interpublic's McCann-Erickson ad network, told Reuters. "But there are some contradictory things. To combine those things is not easy."

The trick, said advertising executives, is how to communicate a single strategic message for a company in a way that can be understood in diverse markets around the world. Only occasionally can those dual needs be fulfilled by a single ad.

"IBM did a pretty good run at it a couple of years ago," said Geoff Thompson, worldwide creative director for Foote Cone & Belding, the ad agency owned by True North Communications Inc . The ads used subtitles to translate the message into a variety of languages.
"It not only made a statement about the IBM brand, but it travelled well," said Thompson. "They were almost done like little foreign films."
Some brands can travel the globe. "Levi's travels well. Coke travels well. Pepsi travels well. Nike travels well," said Thompson. "They've created an image. They've done the work."

But even globally-recognised brands need advertising adapted to local markets. It's not just that people in China speak a different language than those in Germany or Argentina. Each culture carries its own set of values, its own sense of humour that determines what kind of advertising will reach consumers.
"On most brands, including Marlboro, we base our work on local thoughts," said Leo Burnett's Conrad.
The Leo Burnett approach is to have teams of agency employees from Burnett's offices around the world work on creating ads for a single brand.
"Some years ago we produced ads out of the centre, and a lot of people (clients) were unhappy because they felt it didn't fit their local markets," Conrad said.
Now, by using global teams, the agency can work to develop a global strategy and adapt specific ads to local markets as needed.
Even globally recognised brands often find that different ads are needed for various markets.

Alan Pottash, a former chief executive of PepsiCo Inc and now an advertising consultant to the company's Frito-Lay Co, noted how Pepsi learned that ads created in America did not work in Britain -- despite the shared language of the two countries.

"A lot of the syrupy emotion we put into our commercials was a turn-off to the British consumer," Pottash said in a presentation to Ogilvy & Mather at the Advertising Festival. What Pepsi learned was that British consumers responded to a dry humour rather than the feel-good, lump-in-your-throat approach popular in the United States.

Jim Allman, the multinational client director at Ammirati Puris Lintas responsible for the Unilever account, said in a recent speech American arrogance sometimes created problems for multinational companies.

"For every Coke and Kodak, there are many disastrous cases -- and I've been involved in my share -- of American companies that felt because it worked in the U.S. it would achieve the same success in other markets," Allman said.
Even within markets that appear to be similar, there may be sharp differences.
"Proximity of geography doesn't necessarily mean similarity," Allman said. Latin America may look like one market, but a closer examination highlights the differences.
"As a result, advertisers face a big challenge as they try to balance the efficiencies of pan-regional campaigns with more localised ads which reflect individual cultures," Allman said.
Gudmundseth, of Oslo-based JBR McCann, noted that good advertising is based on strong ideas. "Strong ideas can travel anywhere," he said. "But you may have to deliver it differently."

Even within western Europe it is difficult to create successful pan-European ad campaigns. "Very often the commercials developed for Italy we cannot use in Scandanavia -- it wouldn't have the impact," Gudmundseth said.

JBR McCann and two other Nordic affiliates of McCann-Erickson based in Finland and Sweden used the advertising festival to announce a new joint venture designed to win pan-European accounts. The three agencies said they had failed individually to win those clients because each agency was perceived as too local to create ads for a wider audience.
The problem for advertisers is that the high cost of advertising drives companies to seek universal solutions.

"Because of the economies involved we have to search for ... advertising that is accepted worldwide," said Pottash, the former PepsiCo executive. "It's a ying and a yang to get locally based and to get the cost spread over a larger area."
